messages.body_plain:
Hank Green wrote:

> hi statnet team...

>  

> i'm trying to set up statnet on our new 64 bit Linux machine and run 

> into this error:

>  

> "Error: package 'statnet' was built for i686-pc-linux-gnu"

> 

> is there a solution? we considered installing a 32 bit version of R so 

> that we can use statnet but wondered if there was another solution. for 

> example, is there a statnet version compiled for 64 bit machines?

>  



In principle, there is no obstacle to using statnet on a 64-bit machine. 

  However, you'll need to install the package from source, rather than 

use the 32-bit binary package (whence came the error).  I've 

successfully installed sna from source on an Opteron, and IIRC there 

weren't any complications.  I don't think I installed the other statnet 

components at that time, but they should work in the same manner.



To install packages from source under Linux, you'll need to use the command



R CMD INSTALL mypackagefile



where "mypackagefile" is the file containing the source package. 

Assuming you want to do this for the whole system, you'll need root 

access; you can install to a local library directory, however, if you're 

acting as a regular user.  (See R CMD INSTALL --help and/or the R man 

page for details.)  It is also possible to do this with install.packages 

from within R, and indeed that is the default option (where available). 

  Usually, this process is entirely transparent, although things can 

occasionally go wrong (e.g., the compiled code turns out not to be fully 

portable to your platform).  The statnet backends are pretty vanilla 

ANSI stuff, and hence I expect few problems.



Let us know if you need those source packages, and we should be able to 

hook you up....



-Carter



PS. Clearly, we "need" a new 64-bit server....for testing purposes only, 

of course!  ;-)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] question about ERGM terms
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Hank -

Hank Green wrote:
> hi statnet team:
>  
> i'm working on some model hypotheses and wonder if you might point me in 
> the direction of the terms that would best summarize indedgree and 
> outdegree centralization. i'm interested in both network-wide and 
> differential centralization metrics. i've been through the ergm-terms 
> document and am not entirely sure which (if any) of the terms best suit 
> my needs.
>  
> i thought i'd appeal to the masters for guidance.
>  
> thanks for any help...
>  
> and happy fall semester to all reading this.
>  
> hank

All Freeman centralization measures can be written in the (unnormalized) 
form:

C(G) propto cmax(G) - cmean(G)

where cmax is the maximum observed centrality score among the vertices 
of G (under whatever centrality measure is being used), and cmean is the 
corresponding observed mean centrality score.  (I use this trick 
extensively in a soon-to-appear Social Networks piece on density-based 
bounds for degree centralization, but the result applies to any 
centrality measure.)  This means that you can capture centralization 
effects by a statistic which weights the difference between the maximum 
and mean centrality score within the network in question.  In the case 
of degree, this can be re-expressed in terms of the maximum degree and 
density, both of which admit easily computed changescores.

As of right now, there is not a specific ergm term which tracks this 
statistic.  However, ergm was designed to accept user-generated terms, 
and it wouldn't be too hard to hack something like that together. 
Otherwise, this is the kind of thing which will probably get added to 
the main package eventually (since the UCI group is also interested in 
centrality-related questions); AFAIK, however, it's not a priority 
development target in the immediate near-term.

Hope that helps,

-Carter
